strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why learning return distributions can improve expected-return performance. The proposed decomposition offers an intuitive, testable regularization hypothesis.

Experiments cover Atari and continuous-control environments, categorical and quantile critics, and interactions with policy entropy. The environment-dependent interactions are potentially useful empirical observations.
The manuscript acknowledges its KL-specific theoretical scope and the heuristic quantile extension. Pseudocode, hyperparameters, and multiple random seeds provide partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central decomposition has unresolved mathematical limitations. Equation 4 requires an atom at the return mean for epsilon < 1, excluding generic continuous return distributions. CDF approximation does not establish approximation of the KL training objective. Moreover, an atomic target has infinite KL divergence to an absolutely continuous model, invalidating Proposition 3's KL-to-cross-entropy argument in that formulation.

The bounded refinement in Proposition 1 is false as stated. Consider a mixture of 0.75 Uniform[-1,-0.9] and 0.25 Uniform[0.9,1], with c = 1 and epsilon = 0.1. Immediately below the mean, every Equation 4 approximation has CDF error at least 0.65, whereas the claimed upper bound is approximately 0.595.

The claimed connection to entropy-maximizing control is not established. Maximizing model likelihood at the target mean is not generally equivalent to squared-error regression of the model's expectation. Likewise, minimizing critic cross-entropy does not imply maximizing an entropy-augmented policy objective. Equations 8–10 introduce a reward bonus without establishing equivalence to standard distributional RL, whose exact expected Bellman update remains the classical update.

Theorem 1's policy-improvement proof treats the entropy bonus as fixed despite its dependence on the policy and learned return distributions. In Appendix D, Equation 21 effectively replaces the old policy's augmented reward with the new policy's augmented reward without justification. Boundedness alone does not establish this step or the claimed monotonic improvement and optimality.

Equation 12 does not follow from the stated zero-mean residual assumption. Writing the residual as delta, expansion produces a cross term proportional to E[delta sqrt(H)], which need not vanish when E[delta] = 0. Even if it vanished, the specified transformation yields E[delta²] + lambda E[H], not the displayed interpolation with coefficient 1-lambda on squared error. This undermines DERAC's derivation from the proposed Bellman operator.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed mechanism. Comparing scalar and distributional critics changes their representation and training objective simultaneously; return curves alone do not demonstrate entropy-driven exploration or uncertainty reduction. Figure 6 also shows lambda = 0 outperforming lambda = 1 on BipedalWalkerHardcore, complicating the attribution of gains to distributional regularization.

Important reproduction details remain unclear, especially the exact probability-redistribution rule and mapping between experimental epsilon and Equation 4. C51 support settings and the interpretation of shaded variability bands are insufficiently documented. These omissions affect the central ablations. The standard simulator experiments raise no apparent material ethical concerns; the rejection is driven by technical validity and evidential support.
